utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you for being available once again, Dr. Svicevic. Mr. Rodic, are you in a position to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, first of all. We are in a position to proceed. And as we promised last Friday in relation to the journal, I would first like to submit to all the parties the corrected version of the diary with the corrections inserted by Mr. Svicevic so that everyone can have a look. And another thing that we have received as promised is the working notebook, the original copy from Belgrade. And this is another thing that we would like to distribute to all the parties, the Trial Chamber and my learned friends and colleagues from the OTP so that they can compare the original with the copy of the working notebook. Therefore, if you are in agreement, Your Honours, I would like to have the usher's assistance, please, to distribute copies of this exhibit. And then after that, everyone can have a look at the working notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. I did omit to remind Dr. Svicevic of the affirmation he took at the commencement of his evidence, which still applies, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to point out the following: The first new copy was submitted to the OTP earlier and in a timely fashion. Therefore, they can now familiarise themselves with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Last night, actually it was towards the evening hours that we received the alleged second copy. So the Chamber realises that we have not had any glimpse of what is purported to be an original document and only toward the end of the -- I would say early evening hours did we see the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, regardless of that, and although the document was, in fact, submitted to the OTP yesterday in the evening, the same applies as we had said on Friday. The contents of all the notes are entirely identical as in the copied version. The only thing that has been corrected is the order in which these notes were copied from the journal, and this is something that was disputed in cross-examination on Friday. I would also like to have the usher's assistance, please, if the Trial Chamber is prepared to see the original, I've marked it out so you can compare the original copy to the copy that has been delivered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you going to have the witness confirm the nature of what he has done and what we now have, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the journal be shown to the witness and also a copy of the exhibit. Mr. Svicevic, can you please tell us, this booklet that you have in front of you, the working notebook, is that your working notebook, the one that you spoke about and the one a copy of which we have been using so far?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my working notebook. This is an authentic document which I kept in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This working notebook, does it bear some sort of a serial number or a mark?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It bears the number 4, so this is the fourth working notebook that I kept while I was within the composition of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as far as this document is concerned, the one that we've made copies of, these pages from your notebook, did you copy this entry into your notebook following the pages as given here in this document that's been delivered?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did this on Friday, just after the trial finished for the day at the hotel where I'm staying. And the gentleman who provided instructions was present. He provided instructions as to how I should make the entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you confirm that you have copied from your original notes and that you have copied the entries into this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in order to make the text more comprehensible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my proposal for now is that the Trial Chamber have a look at the original of this working notebook and my colleagues from the OTP may as well have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Rodic, if the witness confirm that the order, what he says is the order that is the correct order in which the pages were -- the notes were made. That needs to be clarified, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you please take this document now, look at your own handwriting and the copy. Sir, did you copy these in the same order as given in your working notebook between page 126 and page 138? Can you please compare these.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but page 126 is a page that I copied earlier. As for 128 and onwards, I copied those on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Those copies, do they -- your copies of the notes from the working book, do they entirely correspond with the notes from the journal on the pages marked, the original journal?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is this sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What I'm interested is in what order were the notes made? They were not made in page order according as I understood the evidence of the witness. So we need to know what page follows what page as they are -- as they were written and as we are to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you please now turn to page 126 and 127 of your journal and tell us, which page is it on which you copied the original page 126 by bears the following date in the original journal, the 5th of December? Did you copy that page?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I copied that page, and this is my original handwriting, what you can see here. And that is identical to page 126.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell me briefly, this entry dated the 5th of December on page 126, how does it begin and how does it end?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It begins with the mark, the 5th of December 1991, at Vojnovic, (Delo), area of Dubrovnik, Dubr abbreviation, duel between the Croatian armed forces and the ZNG. There were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how it ends.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ends like this: "Stani Mirovic, so much for the blue."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 127, are there any entries there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look at page 128, any entries there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about page 129, can you tell us about that page? How does it begin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It begins with the following text: SIV, and then the letter L is missing, and then two full stops, team leader for Bosnia and Herzegovina. The second --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the word. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interpretation on page 5, line 24, is says SIV, which means nothing, and this is not a word that was actually used in the courtroom. Therefore, can we please have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, your mic is not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on, Your Honour. My signal says the mic on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. You just haven't a red light any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Svicevic, on page 129, if you can just tell me the following, how the entry begins.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: C. Doyle.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How does it end on page 129?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He had the privilege to meet with A. Izetbegovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where do the notes continue from that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They continue on page 130, and the only entry is "he refers also to Bihac" and this is underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how does that continue?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The beginning?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The new task for the mission is to establish contact with the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last passage on page 131.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "This can be avoided if the mission is allowed to go and see the commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is this an abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: KT, yes, that means commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how it continues on page 132.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 132, it's a note that I made during the conversation, and it says "representative of the SO of Mostar for the JNA and the community to share the fate, be it good or bad."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The next page, 133, how does it begin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have a problem with the way the reservists are behaving and where they are moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The last passage on that page?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In all the communities in which he had talks, there is respect for the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Page 134, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "G. Strugar, column, pursuant to request of the Neum president, he stopped the units at a moment when fire was being opened at us from that area."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Sir, the last passage, how does it begin?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "He wants to separate the JNA," but it's only now that I notice I made an entry here. Instead of the JNA I wrote "the authorities." That was on Friday, so that was lack of attention on my part. "He wants to separate the JNA." And then I just copied "the authorities," but if you look at the photocopy, it says "the JNA," in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about page 135?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you go on, what I hope you will get clear, Mr. Rodic, is whether as the notes were made, whether the notes on 134 follow directly on from the notes on 133, and whether 133 follows directly from 132. That's a point that was in dispute on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you please tell us in which order did you make these notes in relation to the page numbers in your journal? Which were the first ones that you wrote down? Where did you begin writing when you attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put the date when the meeting actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you just please tell us the order in which the notes from the meeting were made in relation to the page numbers in your journal.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken down in a way that is typical of my way of thinking and my way of writing. I always used to write on the odd pages, and then I would use the empty pages to enter any of my personal, additional notes. In this case, you have page 133, which is the continuation -- the continuation is on page 135. So the logical sequence of the last passage from 133, "in all the communities in which he held talks, there is respect for the JNA." And then it follows on the next page: "He's aware of the problem in connection with the disappearance of the pilot." So this is all about the positions put forward by Mr. Doyle. At one point in time, if I may clarify, when this passage was finished, General Strugar joined the discussion and then his contribution on page 134 is something that I put down on page 136, and after that, again, Colm Doyle in response to Mr. Strugar, he continues, and then you have the discussion down from the middle of page 135.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And where can we see a continuation of that discussion between Mr. Doyle from page 135?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It continues on page 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So this was the order in which you made these notes during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Strugar's contribution is on pages 134 and 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid that leaves me then in doubt about the earlier pages. I had understood the witness to be saying that as he made his notes, 130 followed on from 129. And 131 from 130. But it seems that that may not be what he intends to say. So could you perhaps clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, can you please look at page 129. This beginning here, the beginning of the entry, Colm Doyle and Mr. Kogan [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's just here on 129. 129, it's an odd page, and then it continues on 131, another odd page. These are words as actually spoken by Mr. Doyle. And then on page 133, the same thing, this continues from page 131. Page 135 from the middle of the page also continues from page 133, and this ends on page 137, which I think is just like I said. As for Mr. Colm Doyle, his position and his contribution was recorded on odd pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So here we have the beginning of the entry in reference to Mr. Doyle on page 129 as you said. Can you tell us what these entries on page 130 are about in reference to Bihac and on page 132, the president of the SO of Mostar about the JNA and the community needing to share the fate, be it good or bad.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't follow the transcript of these conversations, but talks were held, and I thought that was important. This is something that I considered important, and I thought this would later be subject to regular procedure. These conversations in an abbreviated form would then be sent on to the General Staff. That's what I believed. It's a remark that I made, that during the conversation Bihac was also referenced. But it has been a very long time, and I really can't remember specifically what was being said about Bihac during the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me about page 132.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that, too, shows that I left the even page open. Maybe not always, but very often I left it empty so that I could maybe write down a comment that I had or some ideas that I had. And this was something that I could then later use during the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, does this clarify the matter sufficiently as to what the order was in which the entries were made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the moment, yes. I think inevitably there will need to be some further cross-examination as foreshadowed. If at the end Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of that, if there is still some confusion, the Chamber may need to ask some further questions. I think at least we have the witness's account of the order in which he made these notes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, are you wanting to tender those now, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence abides by its proposal to have this admitted as a Defence exhibit, and can it please be assigned a number, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was originally an objection, Ms. Somers. Is that maintained?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The objection, Your Honour, is maintained. I have asked for purposes of cross-examination, Ms. Mahindaratne will conduct it, but the objection stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we see the original notebook, please. I think before we go further, Mr. Rodic, we ought to get a number of these documents marked for identification. In view of the objection for the reasons originally given, they won't be received at exhibits at this stage, at least, but they will now be marked for identification. Now, first, we have two pages that were put to the witness on Friday in the course of the cross-examination by the Prosecution. I believe they should be received as one document to be marked for identification with a P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just one second, Your Honour. That will be P216 -- excuse me, 218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Next, today is the original notebook which will be marked with a D number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. As for the original of the diary, we already asked Mr. Svicevic. He told us that he wishes to hand over the diary to the Court so that they could see it. But he did also unequivocally express his view that he wanted to keep his notebook once the Court has seen the document. Your Honour, if you wish, of course you can ask the witness yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Rodic. The document will need to be exhibited. In due course, it can be returned. But for the purposes of the trial and until the conclusion of the trial, it will need to remain as an exhibit. I can understand, though, that the witness would have a personal attachment to the document and would like to ensure that it will be returned. The processes can ensure that, and the witness conveniently, I would think, through you can ensure that once a decision is delivered, the document can be uplifted. So it will be --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- marked for identification now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D93 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask, Your Honour, for clarification on the P document. Was that an MFI?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. All of them at the moment are being treated on the same basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now there comes the further composite document, which is both further copies of the notebook, handwritten for ease of reading, a copy of it, the relevant pages, and then a translation of those pages as rewritten from Serbian to English. And that will again be marked for identification with a D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D94 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Rodic, does that conclude the re-examination you planned for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, because the Prosecution completed their cross-examination on Friday. And this document gave rise to a problem, so I thought that perhaps my learned friend of the Prosecution, once all of this was corrected and once the original was brought in, I thought that perhaps they wanted to deal with the corrections, perhaps that they would have additional questions in relation to that in particular, and then I would follow on with my further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the notebook that I gave you, on page 1, I think, there is a quotation of an order that is marked as "strictly confidential." It was used for our everyday work, that particular order. And now I'm asking the Honourable Trial Chamber whether I am relieved of responsibility in that respect; namely, that I'm handing over to you some material that contains a strictly confidential document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are relieved of responsibility because you're handling -- handing over a document in the course of these proceedings. Whether counsel would like to move that the document as a whole be treated as a confidential document as an exhibit is a matter that we will leave for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, following the wishes of our witness, Mr. Svicevic, I would kindly ask to have that document treated in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, do you have any view on the document itself, whether confidentiality is established in respect of the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Having not seen the document, Your Honour, I don't know what it is that's being referred to. In terms of confidentiality, the other particular pages I would assume bear not that same problem. And if the Chamber does have it with the MFI retained, there is a good chance the Prosecution will want to have it looked at perhaps in a more scientific manner, so we would have to seek the ability to do so. I think that could hamper it. Perhaps that one page could be closed off if that is a concern, as confidential, but I think the rest should remain. And there has been no indication throughout testimony that there was any problems keeping it as a regular exhibit. So perhaps just limiting it so that it would not hamper any efforts for further possible scientific inquiry. We would like to have the opportunity to examine it even in the hands of the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it the first page that concerns you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember whether there's something else there, too. But I was primarily referring to the first page. At any rate, I myself believe that this document is my private, personal affair, and if you relieve me of this responsibility, I'm not opposed to having it kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence wishes to point out that as far as this diary is concerned, we would like to exhibit only pages 126 through 138, those that were actually the subject of the examination-in-chief of this witness. So this document basically pertains to those pages only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the moment, only those pages will need to be exhibited. But it may become -- other pages may become relevant. There's no way of knowing. I think in view of the indication just given by Dr. Svicevic, there's really no need for us to make any particular order about confidentiality at the present time. So we'll leave it at the moment as the notebook being marked for identification; and if it comes to be formally received as an exhibit, we'll decide then whether the whole notebook or merely those pages are to be received. Now, Ms. Somers, comes the question whether you think it is more appropriate that you seek leave to reopen your cross-examination in respect of the entries in the notebook in view of the new material, or whether you would prefer the re-examination to be concluded before you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. move.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We definitely do wish to cross-examine, if I understand your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a question of whether you cross-examine now on the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can't cross-examine on the original notebook having not seen it. So there are some questions that we have about the second alleged rewrite, and there is a very good possibility that after further examination of the notebook by whatever means or through whatever persons, there may be other questions. They may be subject simply to argument depending on results. But there are questions definitely about the new rewrite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be dealing with this topic today on one basis or another. And the witness will be allowed to go today when his evidence is concluded. If there should be reason for you to move at some later date for leave to further cross-examine, that we will face when it arises. You may certainly see this document now. My question to you was whether you see any distinction between cross-examining on this document now or whether you would prefer the whole of the re-examination to conclude and then you cross-examine on this document at the end of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Chamber would perhaps allow that the Defence conclude its re-examination, grant us a 10-minute recess to take a look at the notebook, at least preliminarily, after their re-examination, and then permit us to proceed afterwards, I think it would at least facilitate some inquiry that would be beneficial. But I think that's probably the most expeditious way and efficient way, but we will definitely want to ask more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would certainly go one further and say that you may have the document now to examine, and that might give you much longer than 10 minutes while the re-examination is continuing. We don't want to drag this out for time unnecessarily. There are other witnesses waiting, and there's a number of them to be got through this week. Mr. Rodic, I think it's most convenient from a time point of view if you were to proceed to conclude your full re-examination now. The Prosecution will then be able to cross-examine again only on the issue of the document; and if something fresh comes out of that, you will be allowed to further re-examine again on that new issue that arises. Okay? If you could proceed on that basis; and in the meantime, I see the Prosecution have the notebook already. So they can be looking at it as you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I will be quite brief in the additional examination I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svicevic, this document has already been discussed rather extensively; that is to say, the original of your diary, of your working notebook, as well as this copy of this same diary that was copied out in hand because of the illegible handwriting, as you had put it. My question is the following: Let me ask you once again: On the 6th of December, did you keep notes about the meeting and what was said at the meeting that you attended, the meeting that took place between Mr. Strugar and Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you ever change anything in relation to the entries in this diary?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did not change anything. Had I changed anything, I would have changed the date. It is only logical that after the 5th comes the 6th, and then the 6th is when the event took place and it is only logical that this was made, this entry, on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you heard on the 6th of December that there was some fighting in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I pointed that out twice, that this was between 1500 hours and 1600 hours after a telegram was received from the military naval sector, the one that was sent by the crisis staff through the VPS to the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has completed its redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not yet. You may now. Thank you for waiting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Svicevic. Today you tendered to Court a newly written or a second version of the rewritten version of your notes from pages 129 to page 137 of your book. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was pursuant to your instructions. Perhaps not your instructions, but rather the Honourable Chamber's instructions that I wrote...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And now this second version, in fact, reflect the order and correctly reflect what is in your so-called original version of the notebook. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean original copy or the original notebook itself, Ms. Mahindaratne?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The original copy. Thank you, Your Honour, for the correction. The original copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not the evidence of the witness. He's added in the part that was omitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, my point is that this second rewritten version follows the same order that has been followed by the copy of the original version, the alleged original version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It follows page order.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I misunderstood what you were putting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You heard me, Dr. Svicevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, my correction is that this is no second version. It is the same version, but technically it was done pursuant to your request. I used whatever was in my original notebook in order to make my handwriting more legible. And then the slovenly way in which I wrote down some of the notes, well, this is all about my mental principles according to which I work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but my point is -- let me put it in a different way. Do you agree that the version that was tendered before, the rewritten version, and this second rewritten version do not compare in terms of the order that it follows? Do you agree that there is a difference there?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entirely identical. It's only a technical matter between the two copies, only the technique itself is different. But I must point out that in the first copy I left out a page, I think it was 130, pertaining to my commentary in relation to the president of the SO Mostar. So in the first copy I left that out. And in the second copy, instead of writing down "JNA," I wrote "the authorities." So these are small technical errors that may have occurred, but the essence remains absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way, sir: According to your previous version of the rewritten, I'm referring here to the rewritten version, the words "bloodshed, lifting of the blockade, and genocide" are attributable to General Strugar, whereas according to this current version which was tendered today which follow the order of the original version, the so-called original version, those words "bloodshed, genocide, lifting of the blockade" are attributable to Colm Doyle. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have a look at the document. I don't have it front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. That is not what the witness is saying. The witness has tried on several occasions to explain what this is about, and he has explained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, don't you start telling him what he explained at the moment. This is a further cross-examination. If there's a question that is not clear, fine. We can deal with that. But we'll leave the witness who is well able to explain what it is that he's done and what he means.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May the witness be shown D -- I'm afraid I forget what the number was which was given to the marked for id --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please compare the rewritten version which you had tendered earlier on and the rewritten version that you tendered today, and could you confirm that there is a difference with regard to that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have Madam Registrar given the witness D92, the other version, the previous version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, would you please turn to the paragraph which attributes words "bloodshed, lifting of the blockade, and genocide" to General Strugar in the previous version, and the same words now attributable to Colm Doyle in the current version.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are simply not right. In the first version, 12 pages, General Strugar underlined "bloodshed, lifting of the blockade, and genocide". In the original on page 136, the same thing as part of the contribution by General Strugar. In the part that was made tidier, technically speaking, on Friday that I was told to do on page 136 is the same where General Strugar says, and these are comments made by him, that the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if it goes that far, there will be huge bloodshed there, and something about the lifting of the blockade, and also that the population of that area had the additional burden of genocide back from World War II. These are brief notes that I made which now I'm not able to quite put into the correct order in which they were actually said. Therefore, I see no relation between -- no difference between the original version, the first document that I was trying to put in order, what I wrote in my notebook, and the last version, what we see on page 136.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me take you to page 135 of your book. I'm now referring to the copy of the original version, page 135. Do you see there halfway through the page there is a subtitle "C. Doyle"? Those are words that you obviously attribute to Colm Doyle. Now, if you turn the page to page 136, you see the words --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- "genocide, bloodshed, and lifting of the blockade." So when one reads these notes in a sequential order, don't these words "genocide, bloodshed, and raising of the blockade -- lifting of the blockade" should be read as if these are issues raised by Colm Doyle to General Strugar? How is it that you, after 13 years, remember that these were, in fact, words spoken by General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were words or rather subjects that were always discussed for as long as the war operations lasted in the area. The problem of lifting the blockade was a very frequent subject. That was discussed at meetings with the European monitors and the observers around Dubrovnik. As Mr. Colm Doyle was the chief of mission for Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was an opportunity to discuss what was being discussed as a matter of course at the time also within the 2nd Operational Group and in the public media. Should there be war in Bosnia, I remember quite literally, they said there will be blood up to our knees, and also the problem of genocide that was very much in the forefront where the operational group was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are a lot of pits into which Serbian victims had been thrown during World War II. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I just ask you one question: Notwithstanding how it is recorded in your book, how did you remember after 13 years as to who said what when, in fact, your notebook reflect as if these words have been spoken by Colm Doyle? How did you after 13 years remember that they were in fact spoken by General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I have proof. Last night, I followed the logic inherent in these things, and I told you about the odd pages, the pages between 129 and 137, everything that was written down was what Mr. Doyle said. As for the even pages, 134 and 136, those reflect what General Strugar said, as well as pages 132 and 13 -- well, here I have some comments that I wrote down at the time, comments of my own. This is how I write. It's a matter of style. It's how I function cognitively.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Speaking of your writing style, Doctor, what you stated in the course of re-examination today was that when you wrote, you generally wrote -- took down notes of what was transpiring, if it was in a meeting, on the odd-numbered pages, and you wrote down your personal views or observations on the even-numbered pages. That's what you stated. But according to this workbook, on page number 134 and 136, which are even-numbered pages, you have taken down notes of the meeting, what General Strugar said. So you're not being consistent with regard to your so-called writing style, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is perfectly consistent. Under the circumstances, I believed this was the most appropriate thing to do, to record General Strugar's statements like this. Well, of course, now we have something else. We may challenge memory itself, if I'm able to remember thee things after such a long time. But when I was there at the meeting, this was my approach to taking notes. And these notes are absolutely authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Further, your point about what Colm Doyle said were recorded on odd-numbered pages while what General Strugar stated were recorded on even-numbered pages is incorrect considering that on page 130, which is an even-numbered page, there's an entry relating to Colm Doyle. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a reference to Bihac, yes. But this is a personal note that I made. I just wrote it down, just like that. Perhaps it had some sort of meaning at the time, but now it would take a lot of time to explain what the reference was to. I told you what the reference was probably to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is the difference -- now, you say on what you have written down on page 130 is your personal observation, whereas if you take --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you -- could you please indicate as to what the difference is between page 129 where you're allegedly writing down what Colm Doyle is saying and where you state,"he is impressed with the sincerity and the professionalism," as opposed to page 130 where you say you're writing down your personal observation where it stated, "he mentions Bihac as well"? So how do you distinguish between these two entries and determine that one is your personal observation whereas the other is what the person is stating? How after 13 years did you manage to come up with such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're going to something that only concerns my style of writing. I don't think anyone's entitled to do that. There's no one who is entitled to challenge how I function in terms of cognition. I'm perfectly within my rights to function in this way in terms of cognition and to keep this style of writing. All I can tell you right now is that everything is entirely authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I did not intend to challenge your right at all, but my point is how did you determine between these two lines? One says: "He's impressed with the sincerity and the professionalism," and according to what you stated here, this is something that is attributable to what Colm Doyle said on the 6th, while on the next page, your statement that "he mentions Bihac as well," you conclude to be your own observation and not what is attributable to a statement made by Colm Doyle. What is the basis for you to determine one is what one stated and the other is your personal observation?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bihac belongs to territory that was far from the command of the operational group at the time. This is between four and five hundred kilometres. Bihac is part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there was no way that Bihac could be part of anything that had any bearing on the area of the 2nd Operational Group, the area covered by the 2nd Operational Group. Bihac as such was far away from the territory covered by the 2nd Operational Group, and that was why I wrote Bihac. I must have referred to Bihac because there was no need for any comments in relation to Bihac to be part of this discussion. At one point in time he might have said between these words new task or wanting to meet the commanders. When he referred to Bihac, I don't know. But this is my observation. And I must say again it deserves no attention at all because Bihac was far away from the zone of interest of the 2nd Operational Group as covering Bosnia and Herzegovina, part of Bosnia and Herzegovina through the, I believe, 37th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you maintain this as a diary, or did you just merely use this as a notebook to include what information you should write down when, et cetera, or did you use this as a diary?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a notebook for short-term interests and things that I needed to write down. I had three other such notebooks. At that point in time, this notebook was in my possession, and I wrote down, as I said, these things in order to present the most important things that were being said at this meeting in a brief report that was sent on a daily basis to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. However, the notebook in itself as I realised at one point in time, I realised that there was some observations that were relevant to me personally, something that I might decide to write something about. And I've authored some materials concerning the Dubrovnik theatre of war operations, and it should be staged in a theatre in Belgrade next year at sometime hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So if, in fact -- I think on the previous date also you mentioned that you were going to use these books as a basis for a theatre production or a play that you were writing. Now you mentioned that you possibly write about the contents of these diaries. So what is the issue then about the confidentiality of these -- of the contents included in these books that you raised earlier on in relation to tendering this book as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Selection. Selection. The answer is simple, selection. I have the right to make a selection in terms of what could possibly be used in the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You stated just now that you used these books as a basis to send out reports to the General Staff. And also taking a look at the cover, this book has indications of being an official book issued by the JNA. How is it that you kept this in your personal custody after you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official notebook that was officially verified as an official notebook has a particular form. Now, what is the right word for this? There is a kind of thread on it, and then finally it is sealed with a stamp once one leaves. However, I had no need to possess such a notebook. After any meeting, I could have torn a page out or whatever. I had no official duties with regard to each and every page. Actually, in official notebooks that were used in the JNA, only strictly confidential entries are -- in the JNA, if strictly confidential entries are in a particular notebook only, then all the pages are marked, and then there is that thread and that seal that I spoke of. And each and every page has to be there, and one cannot tear out a single page, whereas in the case of this notebook I could tear out a page, I could write down people's names, I could write down the names of people who were supposed to be evacuated, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You just went on to the next point I was going to ask you. Your notebook continues from page 1 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. If I may take a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 1 to page 32. And then from 33 to 37, the pages have been torn out. Is that -- are those the pages that you were planning to use -- or the pages that -- those pages refer to the -- those particular excerpts that you've tendered in evidence. Are there any other pages that you've torn off in this book and I haven't had the time to examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In fact, my colleague indicates that pages 111 to 114 have also been torn off.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason why you tore off these particular pages?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These pages that were torn off were torn off in 1991. Not a single page was torn out later. It was torn out for some momentary needs, when I needed a piece of paper. You see, a significant number of pages there where no entries were made, and then some were skipped. So I point this out once again: This is my cognitive functioning in organised chaos. That is typical of me. On the other hand, if things are not fully organised, then they are remembered better; there are traces in one's memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Doctor, also is it the case that very few pages bear dates that relate to those entries? You have not as a practice dated your entries. Was there any particular reason, or is there any particular reason as to why the 5th December entry is dated and only a couple more are dated? If in fact this book was being used by you as a basis for reports to the General Staff, don't you think it would be appropriate that one would make one's official notes having dated those entries? Isn't this an extremely irregular way of keeping note of one's business activities?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not an irregular way because that day I knew quite clearly what this pertained to and what was supposed to be part of the report. On the other hand, I never thought that this note could be dealt with by a court, that it could be evidence in a court of law. So it just so happened I happened to have kept this, so this is a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: How, then, without dating an entry, how then would you -- can one expect you to determine as to what date a particular entry related to? Did you just rely on your memory for such issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we clarify one thing: It was my understanding that as for the content of the notebook, that is to say, Dr. Svicevic's notebook, that there was cross-examination about that and that cross-examination with regard to that matter has been completed. Now, during the additional cross-examination, questions should be put in relation to the technical aspects of this entire matter. My learned friend is now putting questions about all the things that the head of the Prosecution team omitted to ask on Friday. So I think that that is the core of the matter. Today, we are here to discuss the technical aspects of the copying, and now my colleague is dealing with all these other matters at great length, which is wrong. So could she please restrict herself to the few pending issues. And I think that it is unfair to have my learned friend Ms. Mahindaratne putting questions in relation to what my learned friend Ms. Somers omitted to ask on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, today is the first day that the Prosecution and the Chamber have seen the diary. Your objection was in respect of a question asking about the absence of dates from the other entries. That question could not have been asked until the diary was seen today. So carry on, if you would, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Dr. Svicevic, could you explain as to why all your entries are -- have been written with pen, but only the entry relating to the 5th December 1991 is written with a pencil?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Since this question is being put, then one has to look through the diary very carefully because there are other entries that were written with a pencil, not only the entry relating to the 5th of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the first page was, too. Please look at the first page. I think that's in pencil, too. That's not the first page. It's the order. Have a look at it. Isn't that in pencil, too? No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: As far as I can see --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a look?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness ought to look at the diary to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate if you have any other entries written with a pencil in your diary.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not. But, for example, there are some entries in red pen, for instance. What was written in a pencil -- well, at that moment, I had an ordinary pencil at hand, and that's what I used. Quite simply. And I absolutely stand by what I said, that it's an authentic diary that was kept in 1991. And since then, not a single page has been torn out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage, the Prosecution is reserving its right to cross-examine the witness further once the book has been further examined. That concludes cross-examination for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let me make it clear. You have no right to further cross-examine. Should you seek leave at some later time, you will need to justify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you close your further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic, is there further re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to ask whether I could put a few questions. I'll be very brief in relation to what my learned friend cross-examined about. Could the witness please be given the original, D93, which was marked for identification in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Svicevic, we've taken up a lot of time with this. Could you please take a look at the order, the strictly confidential order that you drew the attention of the Trial Chamber to. Please look at it and tell us what kind of pen or pencil was used to write it down.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pen. But this is page 7. However, on page 6, you can see that again there is an untidy part. It's not very neat, like the entire diary. There's the word "demilitarisation" that is used, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I'm saying now. If you please look at the pages more carefully, were different pens and pencils used and different colours of pen and pencil for making these entries?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's obvious that already on page 11, there is a difference between the pen I used when I wrote the order "the federal secretariat for national defence" that is recorded as strictly confidential. And then later on, it was just the pen I used. On page 21, I used another pen, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There is no need to go any further. Thank you. Tell me, please, you explained that there is also an official notebook in the JNA. And you said that at the end it is stamped with a seal and that there is a thread. I think the thread is called thread of guarantee. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And then when such an official notebook is sealed, there is no possibility of tearing pages out. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the purpose for which it is used?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Counsel is leading the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He is slightly. But if you'd just watch it, please, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What is the reason when dealing with such an official notebook that was sealed, what is the reason why pages cannot be torn out?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kind of notebook is received from a security officer, and that notebook is taken when something should be written in it. When I take that notebook, then it is my duty to hand it back to the person who had issued the notebook to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is there a difference between such an official notebook and this working notebook that you have in your hands now?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in form. There is only the question of essence, that it has this thread and this seal in wax.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would your attitude towards both notebooks be the same or different?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be absolutely different because one has the duty to keep it -- keep that notebook very regular -- very neatly and according to certain regulations. There are regulations governing the use of such a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this original notebook, inter alia, did you make any entries in that notebook that were important in your opinion from the meetings that were held with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik and the representatives of the international community?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have such a notebook, and I wrote down everything in this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you didn't understand what I was saying. In that working notebook, the one that you're holding in your hands right now, are there any entries there that pertain to your communication with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik and the European Community monitors in relation to the meetings you had with them?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've just found some pages now, 47, Di Mistura, then Djuro, then Djuro, that is Djuro Kolic, then page 51, pages 56, 57. They are much less tidy than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have concluded the additional examination I had. And the Defence would like to tender this notebook into evidence as a Defence exhibit, and all the documents that pertain to the notebook; that is to say, the original and the copies, and could they please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The objection, Your Honour, continues. And the Prosecution would ask that it simply retain its status as marked for identification. We may seek -- we'd like to seek to have it examined actually as a document perhaps by a questioned documents examiner. And that would -- upon the -- we would ask for a period of time in which to be allowed to do so, having not had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why should it not be received in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that actually it is -- it may not be what it purports to be, that the Chamber would be burdened with having to go for weight, when in fact, it may not even be properly admissible depending on what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it should eventuate that that later matter is demonstrated, there would be little burden for the Chamber. I think the proper course is to accede to Mr. Rodic's submission and receive the documents. And I take it you would also like to tender the documents that you have put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If the Chamber accepts into evidence over our objection, then yes, of course, and we would make any appropriate motions later. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The documents that have been marked for identification in the course of the evidence of the witness will now each be received as exhibits with the same exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the Court officer is coping with that task, which will take a moment -- are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The respective exhibits are D92, D93, and D94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you leave us, Doctor, could you just help the Chamber with one or two matters. I'm told that you omitted the P exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And P218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding, Doctor, that you say that the notes that you made commenced -- on the 6th of December, commenced at page 129 of the notebook?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, they continued on page 131 as the next page you used?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And then page 133?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't have the document in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Quickly, could the witness see the notebook. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm able to follow now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've gone from 129 to 131 to 133. All the odd-numbered pages.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And are they each notes that you've made of what is being said by Mr. Doyle, Colm Doyle?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would add that the same applies to 135 and 137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was just going on to confirm that. Thank you. So they're all to deal with Mr. Doyle. The even-numbered pages --

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- 130, as I understand you, they're just something you added at some time in the meeting, the note about Bihac.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to say who mentioned that place, Bihac?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is within the sphere of my memory and recollection, but I assume this was a reference made by Mr. Colm Doyle. That's why I -- well, the reference to Bihac, it deserved no further attention, nothing for me to write down, nothing further, because it wasn't within the sphere of interest of the command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why is it on an even-numbered page and not an odd-numbered page if you recall it is said by Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is merely a remark. He makes reference to Bihac. I didn't quote what he said, whereas all the odd-numbered pages mostly reflect his words as sentences. This is a remark that I made, something that cropped up during the conversation with General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. On page 131, partway down the page, there's a heading "C. Doyle."

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why did you put that heading?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this was a semi-formal discussion about the situation in Bihac. After a certain pause, the conversation was continued with words that I believed were noteworthy and deserved to be recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Isn't everything on 131 something that is being said by Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. But as I've just tried to explain, at one point in time, the conversation had been informal and had lasted for three, four, five or more minutes. It wasn't at all interesting in terms of being recorded. So after such an informal exchange, I continued by saying that Mr. Doyle had taken the floor again. Therefore, after an unofficial exchange, or I assume that that was the reason, knowing my style of writing, this was after an informal discussion that lasted for about five or six minutes, and then Colm Doyle proceeded to say something that I believed was worthy of being recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. So there was a passage perhaps five or six minutes' discussion that you didn't note, and then to show that you were starting a new subject matter, you put Doyle's name again? Right.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, if that was a conversation, were there other people speaking as well as Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a conversation of people who held high positions. Myself and the gentleman from the Sarajevo military district was also acting as an interpreter. According to the rules, there were commanders speaking, after all, in this case Commander Strugar and Mr. Doyle who was the representative of the European Community for Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was account on our respective ranks and positions that it was not seen as appropriate for us to join in this conversation. We were there in a more technical capacity, and we were there to technically prepare the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. What would -- was said by General Strugar during the passages that you've got noted on 129 and 131? Where do we find what General Strugar said during that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 134 and page 136. Because in the report that was to be drafted, it was much more essential and important to say what the other side had pointed out, and not in as much detail what General Strugar had said, although, that, too was considered important and that, too, was recorded accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it that you skipped some pages and started making notes of General Strugar at 134 as he was speaking, or was it that you simply made some notes later about what General Strugar had said earlier?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I assert with absolute certainty that I did nothing later. This was all recorded in realtime, everything that was written down from page 129 to page 137 was recorded in realtime during the actual meeting. There were no later additions to this portion of the notebook or any other. Perhaps when I drafted the report that was then sent to the General Staff, I may have remembered a thing or two, something that had not been recorded at the time. And following consultations with General Strugar our assessment was that maybe those things ought to have been recorded in the report that we then sent to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder why then you didn't note on page 128 or page 130 what General Strugar was saying in response to the things that you noted as Mr. Doyle said them, the ones you noted on 129 and 131.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in the meantime, I've made one, two, three, four pages, and in order to avoid going back I always kept this page blank. And I marked clearly that these were General Strugar's words. From page 134 on, he said one or two words, and I recorded those. I don't see that there's a problem there really. This is how it happened. It was the order in which things happened. So I wrote this down on page 134 in order to avoid going back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When General Strugar spoke, you made a heading identifying his name, did you, and then noted what he said?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On 132, can you tell us who said that?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was certainly in reference to Mr. Doyle. This was a digression on his part in reference to previous meeting that he had had with the president of Mostar Municipality. And that was the reason why this additional remark was recorded, and there's no heading as to who had said it. But I can tell you with a very high degree of certainty that this was in reference to Mr. Doyle and his digression to do with the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So 132 is again a note of Mr. Doyle, but you saw it to be a digression. So you've noted it on 132.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the same applies to page 130 where Bihac is referenced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us we go from 129 to 131, 133. There's no note of who said that. That's still Mr. Doyle, is it, as an odd-numbered page?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the next lot of Mr. Doyle is 135. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's another heading of C. Doyle on 135.

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why did you put that heading?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is identical to the previous interpretation that was offered, the two, three, or five-minute one. I can't remember as much, but it was certainly an unofficial conversation that merited no particular notice, nothing to be written down. Therefore, after this informal conversation, Colm Doyle continued to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. So there was another passage that you saw no point of noting, and then when you felt it had got back to a matter of relevance to the meeting, you noted Mr. Doyle's name again and carried on. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The passages you've got noted on 134 and 136, you say they're all General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were they all said at the one time or at different times during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on page 134, one thing you can see following the second passage, there's a mark or a sign. There was a brief pause after which General Strugar was there again. Certainly this was General Strugar's contribution. And at one point probably Colm Doyle had a comment, an additional comment to make which I didn't record. And after an unofficial discussion, briefly General Strugar proceeds. And that's what the mark stands for between the second and third passages. I do notice now however also that there's the same mark between the third and fourth passages. You know, natural conversation always tends to contain some spontaneous remarks being made, unofficial comments being made on the side, spontaneous things, things that do not get written down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So really, those marks in between the passages on 134 and 136 are when there was some unofficial conversation between General Strugar and Mr. Doyle?

utterances.speaker: RADOSLAV SVICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was additional remarks being made. At least I did not believe that it deserved any attention whatsoever. This is the usually kind of thing you get in every conversation, there are certain digressions, longer ones, shorter ones, and these digressions do not necessarily have to do with the subject of the conversation itself. People are paying compliments to one another, making personal observations, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Svicevic, may we thank you once again to the assistance you've given us, and especially for your willingness to stay over the weekend and clear up these further matters and for getting over the original of the notebook. It has helped the Tribunal a great deal, and we would thank you. I'm pleased to tell you that you're now free to go and go back to your home and carry on with what you wish to do. Thank you very much. We will have the afternoon break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It concerned the Chamber that more time was lost over that break than needs to have been. We must be careful with our times throughout the weeks that remain, if all could keep that in mind. Now, you have a further witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, it's Monday afternoon. That must be an excuse for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I accept that kind of excuse. Of course, the Defence would now like to call Mr. Vlado Sikimic as its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would be kind enough to stand and read aloud the affirmation, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your full name.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Vlado Sikimic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, tell us your profession, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I'm a professional military man in Serbia and Montenegro, that is, the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I have been working in the army since the 14th of November 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what education have you had, Mr. Sikimic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I graduated from secondary school and the technical military academy in Zagreb in 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What units did you serve in during your military career, Mr. Sikimic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I am still an active-duty officer of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro since 1980, right up until the present day. I have been working in the logistics units, in the rear. And -- as these were the units that I was trained to work in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you in November 1991? Where were you working?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: In November 1991, I was in the 69th Rocket Base of Herceg Novi at Prevlaka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what unit you were in, or rather what unit did the 69th Rocket Base belong to?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The 69th Base was a component part of the units of the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might the usher show the witness Document D46, please. Would you place it on the ELMO, please, so that we can all see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, on this diagram which represents the diagram of the makeup of the 9th VPS, do you see your own unit there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you do, would you please point with your pointer on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: It was this one, the 69th Technical Rocket Base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't need the document any more. May the record show that the witness pointed to the 69th Naval Technical Rocket Base.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that in November 1991, you were at your duties in the units of the 69th Rocket Base. Tell us, now, please whether at any point in time you were transferred to a new duty.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
