utterances.text: When were you sent to take up a new duty?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Several days before the 15th of November, I received a telegram from the command of the 9th Sector telling me to report on the 15th of November 1991 to the forward command post of the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at the forward command post of the 9th VPS in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of November, sometime before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who did you report to when you reached the forward command post of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I reported to Colonel Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who Colonel Trbojevic was.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Colonel Trbojevic was the assistant commander for logistics of the 9th Military Naval Sector at the forward command post at Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For the record, please, is it Colonel Trbojevic or Trbovic? What is the colonel's name? Because it's not clear enough in the LiveNote. So what was the man's name?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Colonel Trbovic, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what were your assignments and duties at the forward command post of the 9th VPS once you arrived on the 15th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: My duties and assignments were the following: Since Colonel Trbovic was the assistant commander for logistics or for the rear, I arrived there as his deputy geared towards logistics and providing logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what does logistical support imply briefly?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a broad concept, but I can tell you the basics of it. And that is supplies of all equipment, all supplies for units under our area of responsibilities. Then maintenance of all materiel for those same units in our area of responsibility. And third, an important goal, and that is to help out, to act as reinforcement and help the units out in their organisation of logistics and quartermaster services and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where was your office, your actual duty post as of the 15th of November 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: At the forward command post in Kupari, in the building where everybody was accommodated, I had my own office there, a room. An office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember how long you were doing your duties at the forward command post of the 9th VPS? Up until when, the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The 29th of May 1992 with the proviso that the forward command post was not in Kupari throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, how did you procure supplies for your unit -- no, I withdraw that question. Let me put it this way: Which units were supplied and how were you involved in supplying those supplies?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember all the units. For example, the 3rd Battalion belonging to Zdravkovic, Kovacevic's 3rd Battalion, and some smaller units who were in that area of responsibility of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did those units obtain their supplies? Where did the supplies and materiel and equipment reach those units, the necessary resources they needed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Overall supplies and of course maintenance and generally speaking supplies in the broadest term functioned according to the logistics system via the 9th Military Naval Sector or the logistics base of the 9th VPS from Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, at the forward command post of the 9th VPS, did you have any other duties and assignments apart from this logistical work you did?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And which duties were those?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Like all the other people who were in the narrow circle of the forward command post, I was included in the system of shifts of the forward command post of the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, tell us, please, what do you mean by operational centre at the forward command post of the 9th VPS? You mentioned the operational centre of the forward command post a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The operational centre is a system of control and command over all those units which were in our area of responsibility. In other words, that means that it was from that operational centre that we would send orders to all units and other things like that as well as receiving all reports coming in from the units themselves. So it was a feedback mechanism to and from the units and the operational centre in the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, for purposes of the record, you said that in addition to logistics and logistical support, you were involved in other duties, shiftwork, duty officer, and so on. Could you repeat for the record, where did you have the duty to work as a duty officer? In what organ of the command did you do the work of a duty officer, were you on duty?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I was on duty in the operational centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained a moment ago what is meant by the operational centre, what that implies. Now, tell us, please, for all of us to be able to understand, from the operational centre, the forward command post of the 9th VPS, who were you in communication with?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I already said that communication was maintained with all the units in our area of responsibility, every single unit in the area of responsibility that we were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about the resources? What were the resources of the operational centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Communications, and of course topographical maps, rules and regulations, instructions, guidelines, other training material and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what about communications? What means of communication was there at the forward command post of the 9th VPS? Could we just make pauses between question and answer for the LiveNote, please. So tell us again what means of communication was at the forward command post of the 9th VPS in the operational centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: There were radio relay communications, radio telephone communications, and wire communications and lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are these army communications, the kind found in the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of the forward command post of the 9th VPS, was there any other communications network apart from what the operational centre itself had?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, tell us, please, what is meant by a wartime diary or war logbook or notebook?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: A war notebook or logbook is a document that is kept, a record kept in all similar situations and in other situations, and it is especially important at times of war. It is a document recording -- do you want me to go on to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us, what are the entries that are recorded in a war notebook like the one that the 9th VPS had at its forward command post? What entries would be recorded?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: A war --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's no evidence that the 9th VPS actually kept one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I withdraw that question, Your Honour. I'll get to that in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the forward command post of the 9th VPS, was a war logbook kept in the operational centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what is entered into a war logbook of that kind, and what was entered into the logbook of the forward command post of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Again, objection. It's not clear who kept it and basically the procedure by which it was kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you better pin those things down if you could, please, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course. I have had all of that in mind. I am going to ask about all of that. But I am going to accommodate my colleague, and I'll take the order that she considers adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your answer was that a war logbook was kept at the operations centre of the 9th VPS, at the forward command post. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the war logbook of the forward command post of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The war logbook was in the operations centre in the room next to the communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who kept it, or rather, who made entries into the war logbook?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Entries in the war logbook were made by the duty officer at the operations centre. Duty officers were established according to a preset schedule, so every duty officer made entries that were relevant for the war logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, now, what are all the things that are written down in the war logbook of the 9th VPS at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: All orders, directives, guidelines issued to all units in our zone of responsibility are entered into the logbook. What is also entered into the logbook is everything that is contained in the reports from units within the area of responsibility, to put it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What information becomes part of the war logbook?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. That is precisely what I answered a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, since you told us a few minutes ago that you also acted as duty officer at the operations centre at the forward command post of the 9th VPS, did you make entries in the war logbook of the operations centre of the 9th VPS at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was on duty, I, among others, also made entries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the following document distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to register an objection. This document, if it purports to be a 9th VPS document, should have been put to Admiral Jokic when he testified, to put the whole case to him. I think it's a 90(H) violation, and we would object to its use given that it was clear from some of the questioning at the time of cross-examination that information from this document was, in fact, asked or used. And this allegedly concerns the 9th VPS; it was not put to the person who had the longest time on the stand about the 9th VPS. And we think it is inappropriate to raise it at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I answer, or would you first like to have a look at the document yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd be happy if you would put your submission, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first and foremost, as for the document before you, the Defence submitted that in accordance with 65 ter (G) as this is a document that we intend to use during our case. The document is one that the Defence believes should be tendered into evidence. The foundation according to which the Defence would like to have it admitted into evidence is the same foundation as any other in these proceedings and all other proceedings before this International Tribunal. The foundation for admitting this document into evidence is Rule 89, 89(C) to be precise. The Trial Chamber will see already at first glance that this is a document that is highly relevant for this case, and it is a document that is of significant prima facie value. Our request with regard to this document is based on the rules that were set by this Trial Chamber as well in terms of admissibility of evidence. That is actually the jurisprudence that consists of decisions made by Trial Chambers, primarily the Prosecution versus Delalic decision that was passed by the Trial Chamber on the 19th of January 1998, and it was updated several times through decisions made by other Trial Chambers like the one made on the 15th of February 2002 in the case Prosecutor versus Brdjanin/Talic where the appropriate principles were laid. The fact that the Defence did not have this document when Admiral Jokic testified is simply irrelevant. International jurisprudence and the jurisprudence of this International Tribunal does not make this a prerequisite; namely, whether this document was shown to any other witness in previous proceedings during a particular trial. Every one of the parties can show any one of its witnesses any document in accordance with Rule 85(A)(iii) or 83(A)(iv). That is one thing I wish to point out. Secondly, it is not the duty of the Defence to adjust its strategy and evidence to the Prosecution aims. The fact that a certain document was not available at a given point in time is irrelevant. My learned friend invokes Rule 90(H). Rule 90(H) - I assume, but I don't really see what part of Rule 90(H) my learn friend is invoking - is not relevant at all to the situation that we have at hand now. It is the extent of cross-examination that is dealt with there, and also perhaps the cross-examination, namely, that the witness has to be acquainted with the very nature of the evidence involved, but only if this goes beyond the examination-in-chief. There is nothing even similar to that, namely, that the Defence has to present all its documents that it will ultimately tender during its own case to all Prosecution witnesses who appear before the Trial Chamber. This was never the case before this Tribunal. So we believe that this objection is quite unfounded, especially because you will see for yourselves, Your Honour, that this is a document that goes to the very core of the case against General Strugar. Your Honours, the document that is before you is the key document, basic document for any kind of judgement, conclusions, or ultimately decisions in this case. This document comes from military archives. This is a document that was created at the time that we are discussing, and many different things are noted in the document itself. I would also like to remind my learned friend that even the witness that she invoked also on the 26th of March this year, in this courtroom, on page 4.053 said that he had studied this document in great detail. If he had this document, why he did not submit it to the Prosecution within the comprehensive cooperation he had with the Office of the Prosecutor is something that others should consider. However, at any rate, I believe that the objection is quite unfounded and that the document that you have in your hands, Your Honour, is a document that is going to be of crucial assistance to this Trial Chamber in order to rule on matters that my client, Mr. Strugar, has been charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say, Mr. Petrovic, that you did not have this document during your cross-examination of Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you will certainly recall the situation at the time. As my colleague Mr. Rodic said, and he was the one who cross-examined Admiral Jokic, had insight into this document. And on the basis of this insight, numerous information was used and numerous questions were put to Admiral Jokic with regard to this particular matter. You will certainly recall an entire set of questions, if my memory does not fail me, either on the 14th, on the 16th, or 19th of April that have to do with the content of this document. We did not have the document itself; we were aware of its content, though, and we put questions on the basis of what our information was at that time. That would be the answer to your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Why did you not have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a special procedure involved that has to be observed with military archives, and generally speaking in terms of the obligation of the state with cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal and all participants in proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal. Quite simply, that procedure had not been completed by that time. We were given insight into the documents. Of course, we did have a look, and we wrote down whatever we could at that point in time. Physically, the document was not in our hands. So quite simply, that is the situation with regard to this document. May I mention once again in passing that Admiral Jokic himself admitted that he was very well aware of the content of that document as he did say himself on page 4.053 of the transcript, as I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When did you ask or seek to have access to the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point in time, I cannot give you the exact dates. Quite a while ago, that is to say, even before the trial commenced we asked for access to the documents. And that has two stages. One is insight. Then comes copying. That is a rather lengthy process. But I cannot give you the exact dates. However, if the Trial Chamber really believes that this is significant, I will eventually be able to give you a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would have thought from the way you have put your submissions and what we know of the case already that this document would have been one of the first things you wanted to examine in the preparation of your defence. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is the way it was supposed to be somehow. It was a major problem to locate the document itself. However, once the document was located, the procedure was initiated. First, of access to the document; and then the procedure involving the photocopying of the document. You are quite right in view of the nature of the document that this is a key document for the case that we are all dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you did not request to have a copy of this document before the trial commenced?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we asked for an entire series of documents, hundreds of documents, including this particular document. However, until the present day, we have not received a significant number of these documents. We received a significant number of these documents only recently. That is why we are in this situation that we have regrettably been in a position to give our learned friends these documents rather late. For example, the documents that were handed in this morning were received officially only last week. So quite simply, the situation related to documents is as it is. Unfortunately, there are some important documents that we are still looking for, very important ones, perhaps even more important than the one that is before you now, Your Honour. But there are various objective and subjective difficulties that have affected this process which regrettably is sometimes too slow when we think of what is in our best interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, the thrust of the objection made by Ms. Somers, as I understood her, was Rule 90(H). That is, that you did not put the material parts of this document to relevant Prosecution witnesses, particularly Admiral Jokic. What have you to say of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I will say to that is that it is quite simply incorrect. The essence of what the content of this document is is how events evolved on the 5th, 6th, and 7th of December 1991. The Defence challenged what Admiral Jokic said very extensively. And they put it to Admiral Jokic, namely, that his interpretation of what happened is simply not correct. In this way -- what happened on the 6th of December, that is. That is why we presented the nature of our case to Admiral Jokic during our cross-examination in accordance with the Rules. In addition to that, an entire series of concrete questions, and you will certainly recall that, Your Honours, had to do with entries in this war logbook quite specifically. So Admiral Jokic did have the absolute core of the matter put to him; namely, that his interpretation of what happened on the 6th of December, 1991 is profoundly incorrect. That was done throughout the cross-examination. I'm saying that in very general terms. And also in terms of concrete segments of his assertions in terms of who called him, when, where he was, where they were, and all of that can be seen quite nicely from the war logbook. We challenged those sections of his testimony by putting an entire set of questions that had to do precisely with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say that the material parts of the logbook which contradicted the evidence of the Admiral were put to him in the course of his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To a considerable extent, yes, Your Honour. I cannot say fully because you recall all the circumstances that were involved. However, his interpretation of events and in addition to that, his description of individual events were challenged, of course. And this was put to Admiral Jokic. His answer to most of this was that this was impossible and incorrect, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Somers --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just be allowed to add a few words, Your Honours, during the examination-in-chief of Admiral Jokic, I mentioned something on a number of different occasions. He referred to what the substance of the war logbook was, and he told us about how he read the war logbook and how he finished reading it. I referred to a particular page, but I believe I would have been able to locate other such examples of specific pages, but I did not believe that this could have been important. However, if the Trial Chamber believes this to be essential, this should be easy to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Somers, I didn't allow you to interrupt the submission earlier because it was a submission, and you can now have your proper turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think Defence counsel has simply missed the point of 90(H). The fact that something was raised without presenting the document which will be gone into presumably in great detail is not compliance with 90(H). The actual points of contradiction need to be brought up specifically, one can't just have something hovering over the witness testimony and suggesting that that has covered the issue. It must be delved into thoroughly in cross-examination or it is not acceptable. If I can recall from memory, and I may need to actually go back and check, the Chamber inquired of Defence counsel when a certain question was asked about a protest, whether or not a protest was made to the other side. And clearly, these are matters that Defence counsel said, yes, this is part of the case. This is coming from a document that no real cross-examination was carried out on with the leading witness on the 9th VPS. It is a matter of, effectively, foul play. It is clear that the Defence had the information. There's not one request to the Chamber to say, let us come back to this when we get the document. In fact, there was no mention of whether or not it was even in their possession. But it is not a matter that can be taken lightly. The admiral is disadvantaged -- of course, the Prosecution is disadvantaged. But the admiral will have a number of points that he will be attacked and he was never given the opportunity to face or challenge the actual document. Memory alone is simply far too abstract when you're going to get into the kind of detail that appears to be the crux of the cross-examination. It is an essential aspect of 90(H). I would like see the case that is referred to by counsel. But at this point, I think there is no basis. Further, this Chamber, when General Zorc was on the stand, had the same issue raised, where there was a document that could have been put to Admiral Jokic that was not, and the Chamber excluded it, because it was a violation of 90(H). It was not, and it should have been put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, the logic followed by my learned friend and colleague would imply the following, Your Honours: It would mean that we must do a radical rethinking as to what the obligations of the parties in these proceedings are. If what my learned friend suggests were the case, that would mean that everything that the Defence intends to refer to throughout its case should be made available to the OTP prior to the commencement of their case. Or rather, that everything that we intend to show to any of our witnesses, everything that goes to the very substance of our case should be handed over to Prosecution witnesses, too. This simply makes no sense. Your Honours, we shall hand over to this Trial Chamber a whole series of documents belonging to the 9th Military Naval Sector. It is the crux of what we do, of our case. But how can that mean, Your Honours, that we have to show every single document we have to Admiral Jokic? Why on earth would we have to do that? If there is a problem about that, my learned friend is free to put Admiral Jokic on the stand again. And he will be free to address all the issues that the Defence case is about. That is precisely what evidence in rebuttal is about. And then Admiral Jokic will be given a chance to speak and address these issues. But we have dozens of documents that we have obtained in relation to the 9th VPS. I must say I'm surprised when I see that my learned friend and colleague expects us to hand over and submit everything that we had within our case at the time when Admiral Jokic took the stand. This is simply something that is not within the rules, and it's not within the practice. This is an impossible situation. It is for that very reason that the Rules envisage the possibility to put a witness on the stand for a second time to be faced with the Defence case so that he may have a chance to give his own version of events as they unfolded on the 6th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not for a second time, Mr. Petrovic. The obligation of Rule 90(H) in its second paragraph is for the Defence when cross-examining a witness to put the nature of your case to that witness where your case is in contradiction to the evidence given by the witness. Now, that doesn't necessarily require that every document you intend to put in evidence is put to the witness. But you must at least to have put to that witness the nature of your case so that he has an opportunity to answer that. Now, I think that the position that you take and the position that Ms. Somers take are each wide of the mark but in opposite directions. You have an obligation to have put the nature of your case where you felt the evidence of Admiral Jokic was in contradiction of it, and there is a question whether that has been adequately done. But you don't have an obligation to put every document, certainly every original document that may in some way have some relevance to the issues to the Admiral. The problem for the Trial Chamber at the moment is that we don't yet know what precisely is the nature of your case about these matters. And therefore, we're not in a position to know whether you have adequately complied with Rule 90(H) or not. It's only when we learn what it is that you want from these documents that we can start to form a judgement whether what you did put to him in cross-examination was a sufficient compliance with the Rule. If you have not, the only remedy, which is an unwarranted use of time and of inconvenience, would be to allow the Prosecution to recall Admiral Jokic and to go through these matters. But that is not something that should happen as of course. It should only happen where something surprising and unexpected has emerged. But where you knew the nature of the material that you were intending to rely on, even if you hadn't by then with due diligence been able to obtain it, you still had to put, from your knowledge of the documents, what it was that was in contradiction of the evidence of the witness. What I propose as I think the only practical course forward is to allow you to deal with this witness to identify these documents and to identify in his evidence what parts it is that you see to be relevant and material. Ms. Somers, at the end of, that may wish to renew her objection to the reception of these documents into evidence, or she may by then be satisfied that what you want from them was sufficiently canvassed during cross-examination. I don't yet know. We will just have to judge that in due course. So in response to the objection, we won't receive this document yet, if ever, as evidence, but we will allow you to proceed in respect of it and so that we can form a judgement in due course as to whether or not there has been an adequate compliance with Rule 90(H). So if you could proceed, then, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look, Mr. Sikimic, at this document, the document that you have before you. Can you tell us what sort of a document that is.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: This is a war logbook that was kept in the operational centre of the 9th VPS at the forward command post in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the handwritten page, 67, which is part of this document, the upper right corner of the page.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this page, do you see any entries that you made yourself?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which specific entries you made, at what time were your entries made on this page?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I made the entry at 0500 and 0530 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Can we clarify how this witness knows these are his entries. That has not been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: He has just sworn that he made them. But you might like to explore on what basis he's able to recall that, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, were you the duty officer at the operational centre of the 9th VPS at the forward command post during the night between the 5th and 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Since when were you on duty that particular night?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Between 2400 hours and 0630 hours the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hand over duty to at 6.30 that morning?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I handed over to the chief of the operations centre, Frigate Captain Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What does the handover of duty at the operational centre look like?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The handover of duty entails the following: As all the other participants are in the operational centre, and there are no other tasks to be carried out, they get up at 6.00 in the morning, at half past 6.00. The chief of the operational centre, in this case, Frigate Captain Kozaric, for a very long time, takes over personally from whoever was on duty in the following way. He inspects a written document, this document more specifically, and through conversation with his duty officer he finds out about everything that had happened the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, tell us about this entry at 5.00 which you say was made by yourself. Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The last column of this entry at 5.00, whose signature is there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: These are my initials, and I still use the same initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the entry at 5.30? Is that your handwriting there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Again, the initials, whose initials are these?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: These are mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone alter or correct your entry?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the specific times given here in relation to individual entries? Are they correct, and if so, how do you know they are?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The times are correct because this is exactly how we proceeded, and this is what had been ordered, for all units reports to be gathered at 5.00 so that at 5.30 the duty officer coming to take over could be informed as to what had happened the night before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, when do you record the time of a specific entry?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: As events occur. That's when the time is recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that -- I withdraw this. Mr. Sikimic, first of all, what did you record in the first entry of 5.00? Can you please read that out to us.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The first item 3/472, that's the 1st Battalion, during the night, fire had been opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: 3rd Battalion of which brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The 572nd Brigade, the Kovacevic unit. "During the night, sporadic fire had been opened from infantry weapons against the unit from the direction of Srdj. Fire was not returned." If I may clarify, this is a report by the duty organ of that particular unit being sent to us. The next item, the next battalion, also of another brigade, the Zdravkovic Brigade, did not report, so probably later on we were able to find out how and why. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The TO detachment, during the night, there were no problems; the Mokosica command post, everything all right; the Mirogoj duty officer, everything all right. The 16th Border Naval Detachment, everything all right. This entry was at 5.00 exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you record at 5.30 on the same day, the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: At 5.30, I recorded the following: "Sent a report to the duty officer at Korint," which is a code for one of the superior officers, "on the condition of the units during the night, except for the 3rd Battalion at Kovacevic, everything else was peaceful."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 67, will you please be so kind and tell us, do you recognise the handwriting? Who made the other entries on that page, page 67?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: If memory serves well, this is Frigate Captain Kozaric's handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No, not judging by the handwriting. But by the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in what column are the signatures, the last one?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the last one on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of some of the other officers would worked in the operational centre of the forward command post of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a few names.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Frigate Captain Jovo Drljan, Captain Uljarevic, Frigate Captain or perhaps Lieutenant Colonel, I'm not quite sure, Dzelebdjic, and I said that the chief of the operational centre was Frigate Captain, and later Warship Captain Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point in time, I should like to officially ask the Trial Chamber to introduce this document into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Document -- it's the war logbook of the operational centre of the 9th VPS of the forward command post which was handed out to all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I've received your motion. I've already indicated the course we'll take in respect of it. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Is that the evidence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Well, can it receive a -- can it be marked for identification, the document, then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you mean page 67 or the whole of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can mark it for identification with a Defence number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D96 MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, I have a few more questions to ask you. Tell us, please, during the time you were on duty on the 6th of December 1991, were you informed that a soldier of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade had been killed and that two soldiers of that same brigade were wounded?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you, or rather, the information about the death or wounding of soldiers, is that an important piece of information?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There's no time frame asked about when any information might have been communicated. It's just a rather broad question. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question was prefaced when he was on duty, but that begs the question when was he on duty other than 5.00 and 5.30. Perhaps you might ask when he commenced and finished duty that day, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I'll ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From what time to what time were you on duty, Mr. Sikimic, on the 6th of December 1991 in the operational centre of the 9th VPS and its forward command post?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I've already answered that question, but I can repeat my answer. From 2400 hours to 6.30 hours in the morning of the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During that time interval, did you receive information that a soldier had been killed belonging to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, other rather that two other soldiers were wounded from that same brigade.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Once again, let me ask you again, would you consider a piece of information like that to be important information?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely so, important information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you, had you received information of that kind, introduced it and entered it into the logbook, war logbook?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, in the course of my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was information and reports of this kind, were they recorded as entries into the war logbook of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. And even less important information would also be recorded. So information that was that important would certainly have been entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The operational centre of the 9th VPS at the forward command post, during the time you were the duty officer, did they receive a report to the effect that an attack had started with some of the units of the 9th VPS within the environments of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You as the duty officer in the operational centre, did you perhaps receive a report that the attack of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade had launched an attack on Srdj?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During the time you were on duty once again, were communications from the command post of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade working normally?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this can be seen from the logbook. They called in at 0500 hours, and I noted that down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, during your time as duty officer, did Admiral Jokic contact you at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you call Admiral Jokic during the time you were on duty at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During your term of duty on the 6th of December 1991, did you convey any orders to subordinate units within the composition of the 9th VPS at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody issue orders to you to ask or establish a contact with some higher officers of the 9th VPS during the time you were on duty during the 6th of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did Admiral Jokic ever sleep at the forward command post of the 9th VPS in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, no, he did not. And I was there for quite a long period of time. I never saw him spend the night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The question of ever sleeping is one that doesn't have appropriate temporal limitations. The man only came into the area on the 5th of November, and I think that the observation must be limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how else it could be understood. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- you might want to explore it expressly a little further, Mr. Petrovic, to give some substance to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During the time period that you spent at the forward command post of the 9th VPS, and you've said that that was from the 15th of November 1991 onwards, up until the 31st of December 1991, did Admiral Jokic ever spend the night and sleep at the forward command post of the 9th VPS during that time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: For as long as I was there at the forward command post, during that entire time, Admiral Jokic never spent the night, never slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have Madam usher's assistance, please, to distribute the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, can you tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: This is the usual type of document, a report, about logistics, or rather from logistics to the superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who is this report addressed to?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The report is addressed to the command of the 2nd Operational Group as it says, and the command of the Military Naval District, but to the forward command post which I think was at Vis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: This document was issued by the deputy commander for logistics of the 9th VPS, Colonel Petar Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the front page of that document, please, and number 1, the fourth point. Can you read that out, please, tell us what it says.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Number 4 says the following: "The 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade had a full complement in the village of Brgat. It had 80 pieces of mines for 120-millimetre mortars, 40 pieces of rockets, 4 Polo 9 K 11, 60 pieces of signal bullets, 26-millimetre type, and 40 pieces of rockets." This is a mistake here. It says "mekata," but it should be "raketa metaka," which is bullets, for the T-55 100-millimetre weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, is this the standard type of report that would be compiled and sent out to the superior units?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to tender this document as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D97.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher show the next document to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the document please be placed on the ELMO for the benefit of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, what kind of document is this?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: This is also a daily report pertaining to logistics which was sent out to the superior commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what is the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: It is dated the 5th of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: This document was issued at the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The question is who issued it, and the response was at the command. I think it's not responsive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikimic, you said that it was issued by the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector. Could you tell us who issued it, who at the command.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: By the assistant commander for logistics, Colonel Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 1 of the B/C/S version of this document, would you take a look at that, please, and look at number 1, point 1, where it says "the forward command post of Kupari was replenished." What with? Could you tell us what with pertaining to this report?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: It says plastic explosives, 10 kilograms here; AE1 bombs, 12 pieces; AF1 bombs, 12 pieces; 'Zoljas,' 10 pieces; and bullets, 7.9-millimetre for snipers. It just says 7/9, but what it means is 7.9-millimetre pieces, one crate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this exhibit as a Defence exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is D98.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That was the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Somers, it would be convenient to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. It certainly would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sikimic.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, just make sure I'm not drowning out the microphone, here. Mr. Sikimic, for your entire military career, have you been involved with the logistics side of duties?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout my military career, I have been involved with logistics, logistics, support for the rear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in connection with your assuming the role within the IKM at Kupari around November 15th, had you been a duty officer before? Had you had occasion to handle the functions of duty officer?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Wherever I've worked. This is a perfectly routine job for every professional military officer, being the duty officer or the operations duty officer is a perfectly normal thing for a professional military officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your operational training would include what, if anything?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: May I just be allowed to clarify one thing: There is no specific training for being duty officer. Whoever is in a specific place at a specific time has already been trained to, among other things, be the duty officer in certain places.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Had you familiarised yourself with the various issues, if any, surrounding or concerning the units that were in the area of responsibility at the time, say, from the 15th of November? And specifically looking up to 6th of December, found yourself?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your question. I was familiarised, not on the 15th, but as of the 15th of November. As for your questions in relation to my training and in relation to the reason why I had been dispatched to the forward command post which was to provide logistical support for the units, it's within the framework of that issue, providing logistics support for the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And had you become familiar with what was occurring, what stage the actions in that area were at at the time you came in to the area?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: As for the specific stages, no, I had not become familiar with those. But that was not part of my remit, my job description. But I did become familiarised with the current situation and what was to follow. Again, I must say, within my remit, my job description, which is the logistics support for the rear.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If I can ask you -- I'd like to ask you a question from the document that was dated the 4th of December, if I can ask my colleague Ms. McCreath to pass it to me, and I'll give you the number. It is D97. Let me see if this is the one I'm... Do you have it in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be good enough to turn to or to put your attention to -- under item number 1. It says, in English, "40 pieces of rockets for Polo 9K11." That is Maljutka, is that not? That refers to a weapon, the Maljutka?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. I'm finished with that document. The diary, the diary that has been marked for identification as D96 - thank you - I'd like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at some of the points that are on page 67, to which your attention was directed, I'd like to ask you, have you looked at the diary generally before you came here?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, at the entry of 6.50, 6.50, it says "Captain Kovacevic" - I'm reading you from the English, so you'll have to accept whatever translation was given to you; I apologise if it isn't as clean as the Serbo-Croatian version - "fire was opened by the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade on Srdj. He decided alone to do so with MB120." What is MB120 referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: This is an artillery weapon. It's a mortar. MB120 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking a bit further down,"7.30. At 9.30, Kovacevic is to call Jokic in Cavtat." And then looking at 7.40: "I transmitted the order of the commander of the 90th VPS to Kovacevic. However he is already in a situation where he cannot cease fire because he has already emerged on to the mountain range in the region of Gruska Glava, Jevica. He will see what can be done." Now, whose entry is that, if you are able to tell us? Do you have the Serbo-Croatian version?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I don't think I could speak about someone else's handwriting. All I can tell you is that this is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you turn to what is page 68, please, 9.00 entry: "Precisely determine who and when opened fire. Captain Kovacevic is to write a statement to the commander." Is it clear to you who may have put that entry in?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said a moment ago, at the forward command post, the duty of the operational centre was Frigate Captain Kozaric. Whether he was the one who made this entry or someone who was the duty officer at the time I really can't say. There are two possibilities. It may have been him or someone who was on duty at the time. Now, who was on duty, where, and what I really can't say anything about these.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where is in the Serbo-Croatian edition and also in the English translation, there is a little symbol. It looks like a Greek letter with the number 107 after it. Do you see that? It would be next to the -- let's say, 8.55 entry on page 68.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be able to decipher and explain what that entry means, please? There's a symbol attached to it, its meaning.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No. No, this looks like a summa, summarum 107, but what that is in relation to, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a second. I want to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, during the time period that you are on duty, up to -- well, the only entry I think that would be necessarily within your time frame would be the last entry of 5.30 - would that be correct - on page 67 for that date, 5.30?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: There is no -- there is nothing transmitted about death or injury to any units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In fact -- excuse me. It was -- the reference is to occasional fire, occasional fire.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. But if I may be allowed to clarify, sporadic fire, but on the basis of this report and what I was told and what I recorded, sporadic fire from infantry weapons against that particular unit and from the direction of Srdj by the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. The entry that I think you identified in chief, a signature of Mr. Kozaric, which is evident from the -- at least it is shown on page 68, if his signature appears as writing during the shift after yours, does that indicate to you that he, in fact, would have made other entries that were listed between the end of your shift and anything from the next shift, whether his name appears there or not, if it appears in two places, if there are other entries where it might be absent, would it suggest to you it would also be he, Captain Kozaric, who would be making those entries if it was still during what would be his shift?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't believe the answer is clear because you can't tell which two places are being referred to. May this please be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For example, on page 67, you see entries that have Captain Kozaric's name, let's say at 7.15 or 7.30, and you don't see it for 7.40. But would it be a logical -- would it be logical that he would have been the individual making the entry as well? If his name appears right above the 7.40 entry and if it were he on duty, would it be he to the best of your knowledge who would be making those entries?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that at all. After duty, I left the operational centre, and I started going about my own tasks from my own area of activity. It would have been logical for Kozaric who was the next in line to sign it, but this may also have not been the case. This would require an analysis to be carried out by a handwriting expert. He may have been the one who signed it, but he didn't put his initials there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That happens from time to time, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it does, in haste. You just forget. You forget to place your initials there. This wouldn't be the first time for something like that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And particularly if there are events going on that are perhaps out of the ordinary. Right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I could agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what are the shift times? You worked from 2400 to 6.30. How did the shifts run? What were they broken down in hours?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The forward command post in the narrow sense of the word, the core of the people who were there, all the people who were at the forward command post, the total of the people who were there, I'm talking about between 10 and 15 people as a rule, and those were then broken down in shifts covering the entire day except if someone was absent on whatever mission, all the men were inside and around the operational centre. Every six hours, according to a predetermined schedule, they would take turns, and you knew who was on duty. I can't say myself, because I only arrived later, what the schedule was or who had drawn it up. But I suppose it must have been one of the chiefs of the operational centre who had drawn up that particular schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at the entry on page 67 for 7.05, it is -- it reads: "I called Kovacevic. He is still opening fire on Srdj. I ordered that except in the case of fatal situation he is not to open fire with the 120-millimetre." Now, in the original, in the Serbo-Croatian original, there is a name next to the entry. Would you be able to tell us whose name it is, please? It's not indicated in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The name is the same. But it's about the initials. The initials belong to Mr. Kozaric in relation to this entry at 7.05.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in relation to -- let's see, we asked you about 7.15. "7.15, positions on Strincjera," I think that's possibly an English typo, "were hit from Srdj around 600 hours with Zoljas and MB82s." And whose name appears in the column on the right next to that entry?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand you. Which time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The initials are also those of Frigate Captain, Captain Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where that night Admiral Jokic --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. But I believe I've pointed this out earlier. It's been a long time. It is my impression that these are the initials of Mr. Kozaric, but I can't see with certainty. The only thing I can speak about with any degree of certainty is my own signature. It's difficult to fake since my handwriting is really poor. In all likelihood, I can tell you that these are his initials since Captain Rade Kozaric was the one who took over at this time, that is given here, and continued to record the entries.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. We were talking I think for a minute about 7.15, and then let me just make sure I've got you -- 7.30 on page 67, the entry for 7.30: "Kovacevic is to call Jokic - now I'm not sure, in English there's a -- "Kovacevic is to call Jokic in Cavtat." Are you able also to assist us with what you believe to be the set of initials, or whose initials you believe it to be, or perhaps name is in the column at the end of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Just as I've already said, Frigate Captain Kozaric, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I've asked you already about 7.40, although it doesn't have the name or initials in the column. Let me just take a look at the -- 7.47, please, on page 67. It says: "I transmitted to Captain Blaza Jovanovic to order Colonel Jankovic and Lieutenant Colonel Bojovic that an absolute cease-fire is to take place today at 1200 hours." Are you able to assist us with whose name may appear or is most likely to appear in the column at the end of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I think the answer is the same like a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification: It is -- it appears these are not just notes that are taken down by a man sitting behind a desk. These are entries that bear a seal, do they not, a stamp of the -- well, if you can tell us what stamp is on there, that would be helpful. Do they bear a stamp? Does each page with entries bear a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I explain what this is about, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let the witness -- you may wish to add something later, Mr. Petrovic. The witness can deal with the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember exactly, but I don't think that there was a stamp on every page of the war diary. This can be a stamp from something else. Maybe a certification of the photocopy or something? Anyway, I cannot say anything about the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you just help us --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Can I just explain this, may I? Usually either on the first page or on the last page of the diary, there would be a particular text stating that this document contains such and such a number of pages, and then it is given a seal with the person who is entitled to use the document. And I'm not sure that there was any such thing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On this particular page, if you look at page 67, for example, do you see a stamp? Does your page have a stamp on? Let's say next to the entry for 5.00, can you read it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read the stamp.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't. It's not legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Flip the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We don't want to interrupt the witness. I think I know what you're going to say. I've worked it out already, but we've...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the next page, it is legible. This is a stamp from the military archives that probably gave this document. You will have to ask the person who brought these documents. But the stamp on this page is that of the military archives. So it's the military archives that allowed this to be photocopied, and I assume that this document is still in the military archives. So that's the stamp that you're asking me about, and it has nothing to do with the situation in Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, these reports in their format were sent to the 2nd Operational Group, the 9th VPS. Correct? Commands of?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Would you please explain that. Could you explain what report you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Any of the entries, in other words, the entire set of entries would be directed both to the 2nd Operational Group command as well as the command of the 9th VPS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No, no, not this one. A special report was made. The commander or the head of the operations centre sent this precisely to the addresses that you just mentioned. So it's not that this particular information was sent, but everything that was essential from this and other pieces of information, that is what was sent precisely to those addressees. And then that would be signed by the sector commander or his deputy or the chief of the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what particular duties a duty officer actually attends to besides, for example, taking down communications? What other duties were part of your assignment or taskings in that function?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No other duties. The duty of the duty officer is precisely to convey to all units in our area of responsibility of the forward command post the orders of the commander or the orders of anyone else who may be in charge. And it also works in the opposite direction, to receive all reports and all other information from units within that zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The night between 5th December and 6th, do you know where Admiral Miodrag Jokic was, where he slept? Do you know personally?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I absolutely know that he was not in Kupari at the forward command post, and I really do not know where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you about a few pages further, if I could, please. If you can look, let's see -- sorry. I thought I had it marked. I don't mean to take your time. On page 68 at 11.07, please, it says: "Stop the activities of POC; at 11.15, stop all further actions. Absolutely cease all action against the town. Transmitted to Kovacevic personally." What do the abbreviations POC stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: What time entry are you reading out?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: 11.07. Do you see it at 11.07 on page --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: No. Oh, I do, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What would that abbreviation stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It is not a military abbreviation. It's not one of the regular military abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: So you are not familiar with that particular abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it is logistics company, Pozadinska Ceta, but this is not the way to write it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Looking at page 70, please, 70, there's a -- at 13.05, there is an entry -- there are two actually. And one of them has a remark in the right-hand column where it says "captain of the battleship, Zec." What does the name appearing in that right-hand column referring to when it says "captain of the battleship, Zec"? What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Precisely what you said. These are the initials of Battleship Captain Milan Zec.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Does that mean that that is the person whose words are being communicated, that it is coming from that person? In other words, this person is not at the duty station, but the communication is coming from that person. Is that what that would mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand what you were saying. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sure. It says "captain of the battleship Zec." Does that mean as far as you know, your understanding of how these entries were made, that the entry was made by Zec, the actual physical entry in that log, or does it mean that a message was communicated or conveyed by Captain Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have one suggestion actually by your leave without interfering with the question. I don't know if the witness is looking at the original or the copy into B/C/S. Perhaps it could be better if he looked at the original. Oh, I see, he is looking at the original. I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer now. May I? According to what is written here, it means that the person who made this note put his initials here. I cannot recognise everybody's handwriting of all the people who were there, but theory says, and this is what we did in practice, too, the person making the entry should put his initials there as well. So now I cannot tell whether this is this person's or that person's signature or initials.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Or if, in fact, it was the person himself or a message conveyed on behalf of the person. It's not clear from here. Is that what might be?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I can just give my own opinion, that that is the -- those are the initials of the person who received and conveyed that message. Because if it was a conveyed message, then the person would put his message and entry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On page 70, at 13.49, let me see if I can read it, page 70, 13.49, Frigate Captain Handzijev was ordered to call Bileca and Trebinje and to immediately order Colonel Kovacevic to come to the IKM KVPS. Can we identify a few people there. Who is Frigate Captain --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Frigate Captain Handzijev was the duty officer, or rather the head of the operations centre. Now, I'm making an assumption, but I'm 99 per cent sure of this, head of the operations centre of the 9th Military Naval Sector in Kumbor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And the reference to calling Bileca and Trebinje, what to your knowledge was at Bileca and Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I assume that it is superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who is Colonel Kovacevic? Do you know that, Colonel Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I do know, though, that in the command of the 9th Military Sector there was a Colonel Gavro Kovacevic, if I can remember correctly, who was one of the assistant commanders of the 9th sector. I assume this is a reference to him since Handzijev is being ordered to find him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You answered my question of what was at Bileca and Trebinje. You said the superior command. Which superior command is at, if you know, Bileca and Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not say supreme command. I said superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: That's what I just said in English. Perhaps it was translated incorrectly into your language.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm assuming. I have to point out once again that I'm an officer who was involved in logistics. And I'm afraid that you are not going to have much use as far as I'm concerned for matters such as drawing maps, unit deployment, because in practice I really dealt with logistics only so I don't know very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't want you to draw a map. I just want to ask you -- when you say, "I assume that it is the superior command," about Bileca and Trebinje, which superior command are you referring to? What did you have in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me, please, just a point of clarification, what is the situation? Do you have bunkbeds? Is there a sleeping accommodation in the operations centre where you were working at Kupari? Could you give us a physical description of how it is? If someone is sitting at the duty desk, where are the other persons whom you described as being around the operations centre or in?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The operational centre was in the hotel building. The operational centre itself consisted of two rooms which were joined. They weren't separate. In both these rooms in one we had the communications centre, and the war diary where everything was entered and recorded as we had discussed it. In the first room which was a larger room, there was a big table with some other things, maps, instructions, and other things. And the people were there at all times. And each of them was engaged in his own line of work. There were no beds. We all had our own rooms, or rather offices where we saw to those matters that didn't have to be seen to in the communal room, if I could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And when you say that there were people there at all times, do you mean there were persons other than the man at the desk or the woman at the desk, let's say the man, at the duty desk present 24 hours a day, 7 days a week? There was always another person in the duty -- in the operations centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
