utterances.text: I didn't say it was next to the duty officer, but in the first room, and the people spent their time in the operational centre in the first room mostly, whereas the communication equipment was in the second room linked and connected to the first room. And that's where the duty officer had to be as a rule or some senior officer who was able to record events in that particular document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As between the first and second rooms which were connected, was there always a second person around and available in the event something were to come up or something were to happen to the man at the duty desk taking communications?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that a moment ago. Most of the time everybody was in the first room, except from 2400 hours till morning when there was a schedule as to who was supposed to be where when.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me just a sec.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: On page 70 -- I'm sorry, I was asking you a question. I dropped it off in midpoint. I was interested in the other point. Explaining a little bit more, when it said that Colonel Kovacevic was to come to the IKM KVPS, where was he to come to? What did that mean? You just explained who Frigate Captain Handzijev was, you told us about Bileca and Trebinje, and you mentioned Colonel Kovacevic, and he was come to the IKM KVPS. What location is that referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: That means in Kupari at the forward command post which is where the IKM of the 9th VPS was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Which is where you --

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Specifically, in Kupari, the operational centre. And as it didn't say anything else, doesn't say anything else, that's what it implies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about another... Sorry, I've lost the area I was looking for. Could you go back to page 66. That is actually an entry from the 5th of December. Where it says the time 19.40. Do you see that on page 66, 19.40, the entry? It says "Dubrovnik" -- you don't see it? Let's make sure you have it in front of you. Page 66.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: I see, 65, 66, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You have it? Okay.

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: 66. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you look at the entry for 19.40, please. 19.40. It says "Dubrovnik Crisis Staff to the command of the VPS Boka, we ask that you certify the unimpeded and safe passage of the ship 'ARGOS II' for the talks scheduled tomorrow at 1000 hours in Cavtat." And it says, "Dubrovnik Crisis Staff." Now that entry indicates that the message came from Dubrovnik Crisis Staff to your duty station? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: It was sent to the command of the military naval sector. Now, why it was sent to the IKM, I really can't say, the forward command post, because that didn't come within my remit at the time nor was I engaged in affairs of that type. I was just able to convey something that had been -- that I had been ordered. But yes, from the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, that's correct. But the command, not the IKM, the forward command post, but the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If you look at 19.42 on that same page, "KVPS Boka, Dubrovnik Crisis Staff: We permit and guarantee the safe passage of the ship 'ARGOS II' on 6/12/1991 on the route Dubrovnik harbour, Cavtat harbour, Dubrovnik harbour from 0900 hours until the arrival to the Dubrovnik harbour." And it appears to signed of command of the VPS. Whose name, if you can tell, if you're able to see, appears in the column, the right-hand column?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: In the tenth column, there is nobody's name. There is just an entry, a remark, stating that the text was dictated and handed over to Frigate Captain Handzijev in Kumbor. That mean this document, this text was handed over, and they were supposed to send on this exact message.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we move basically on to your area. And the entry -- the entry at 5.30 on the morning of the 6th on page 67, what is Korint? It says DO -- if you turn to page 67. And it's an entry that has your initials, I believe, by it. What does "DO on Korint" mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: DO Korint means duty officer of some unit bearing the name of Korint or Corinth. So it was the coded name for a particular unit, and that particular coded name was Korint, to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Do you know what that unit was?

utterances.speaker: VLADO SIKIMIC
utterances.text: Duty operations officer. I really can't remember. These are coded names for units. There were a lot of -- a lot of time has gone by since then, there was a lot of duty work, so I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I inquire of the Chamber. I have maybe another 15 or so minutes that I'd like to use. But will the Chamber be addressing any administrative matters this evening? I would otherwise ask to have tomorrow. I believe we're starting at 9.00, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you will not finish tonight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will not. I need a little bit more time tomorrow, but I believe we were informed that there might be some admin matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can leave the evidence then until tomorrow. I must ask you, Mr. Sikimic, if you would return tomorrow at 0900, 9.00 in the morning, when we will be continuing the evidence. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And there is a question that might be able to dealt with tonight. The witness could go now if he likes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to just briefly to raise a problem and ask for your assistance in solving it. The accused informed us that tomorrow morning he has a dentist's appointment. Now, I do not know whether we know anything about that and how we're going to get round that and solve it in view of the fact that we had a situation previously where we were supposed to sit in the afternoon tomorrow. I'm just putting the problem to Your Honours. I don't know how to go about solving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you know what time is the appointment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 8.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have two choices, Mr. Petrovic: Clearly your client should go to the dentist. We either commence at, say, 10.00 and sit a little later into the day, or we sit again at 2.15. But the problem with 2.15 is that it keeps your client up late, and so we've tried to move to the morning as often as we can. Would you just confer as to whether a 10.00 start would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a previous dental appointment which had to be put off because the dentist had a traffic accident apparently. I feel that faced with the situation, the best idea would be that the dentist's appointment go ahead at 8.00, and that we go at 10.00 as you have just suggested. And then if necessary, to go on for longer hours in the afternoon. I think that might be the best solution, as you yourself stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume tomorrow at 10.00 in the morning, 10.00, not 9.00. Understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can go with the court officer now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The quick procedural matter I wanted to raise was there's a Defence motion for a videolink for the taking of the evidence of one witness, and that's wanted for next week. Given the time that's necessary to arrange these things, the sooner we deal with the motion the better. Is there any objection to the motion, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The initial reaction of the Prosecution, Your Honour, was that -- I mean, it is viva voce and it is live testimony. But the difficulty occurs sometimes with exhibits, and particularly if we are given really very late whatever information the Defence has or wishes to convey to us about the witness. So whereas distinguishing, from let's say, Dr. Blum's testimony where everything was well in advance provided, that is not the case with some fact witnesses. If on humanitarian ground, and again, not meaning to sound skeptical, but we would ask perhaps for some documentation to the effect that this is the case or a representation as to what the nature of it is. And if the Chamber is satisfied that there really is a medical urgency or a medical need, we would not stand in the way of the witness testifying, if it's important that the evidence be heard. But obviously, the first preference is for live, in-court testimony, particularly where there may be documents. And if there's some way of confirming what the actual nature of the situation is ... Could it be handled with a one-day in, one-day out, quick turnaround time the witness, because the witnesses seem to be going fairly quickly here. Would that also accommodate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't be relaxed with the quick pace of progress with witnesses. The nature of the condition of the witness and the witness's wife, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be allowed to respond all the three points put forward by my learned colleague. The first point is this: With respect to the documents that we intend to use through the witness in light of the fact that some of the documents were handed in later than usual, than is customary, all the documents, if the Trial Chamber agrees to our request, we will have at least -- the documents will be sent to the Prosecutor at least seven days in advance so that they can get -- become acquainted with all the documents. And there will only be two. I'd like to make that clear straight away. The second point I would like to respond to is to say that it has been our practice in the previous situation when the Trial Chamber agreed to have a videolink testimony for the Prosecution witness, despite the skepticism we displayed, did not imply the need for medical documents to be shown to confirm what was written in that request. This kind of practice was not asked for, nor was it availed of in the Prosecution request for a videolink. And now to go on to point 3, Your Honour, this is a witness who is a retired person. He has a wife who is sick and who undergoes constant medical assistance. And she is at the medical academy in Belgrade. We can supply the medical documents referring to her, and she is undergoing constant therapy. But I'm afraid I'm not sure that this will be possible over the next 24 hours that we have. We need at least 24 hours for preparing the videolink, but we can do our best to come by those documents and thereby support the assertions made in our request. And let me also say that the witness is a very important witness, and I assume that were it not for these problems, the witness would appear in this Court. And our request and all the circumstances surrounding our request is fully in line with the practice that this Tribunal has resorted to in the past. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the circumstances, the Trial Chamber is prepared to deal with the motion now and to order that the testimony of the witness will be given by videoconference link, but it does take up your suggestion, Mr. Petrovic, and it requires that any documents that are to be used by the Defence in the course of the evidence of the witness should be provided to the Prosecution seven days before the evidence is led. That way, we will minimise any possible inconvenience to the Prosecution from this arrangement, but will allow you to meet the needs of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume, then, tomorrow at 10.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of July, 2004, at 10.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
